topics.title: The Islamabad Memorandum ends the 2026 Iran war
topics.hook: On 17 June 2026 the US and Iran signed the Islamabad Memorandum, ending nearly four months of war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a crisis with a direct line to India's oil bill.
topics.story:
The war began on 28 February 2026, when Israel and the United States launched joint air strikes on Iran that killed the country's supreme leader and several senior officials. Iran retaliated, Israel struck Lebanon in parallel, and by April the United States had gone further: on 13 April, President Trump ordered a naval blockade of Iranian ports, cutting off the country's main route for oil exports.

Pakistan stepped in as mediator. A first round of talks in Islamabad on 11 and 12 April produced only a fragile two-week ceasefire and collapsed within days. Qatar joined as co-mediator, with Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Egypt facilitating on the sidelines. It took two more months of on-and-off negotiation before Pakistani prime minister Shehbaz Sharif announced, on 12 June, that a final text had been agreed.

The signing itself was split across three cities. Iran's president, Masoud Pezeshkian, signed in Tehran. Shehbaz Sharif signed in Islamabad, lending the memorandum its name. Trump signed remotely from the Palace of Versailles, where he was attending the G7 summit at Evian and had dinner that evening with French president Emmanuel Macron.

The 14-point memorandum stops the fighting on every front, including Lebanon, and reopens the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway through which roughly a fifth of the world's traded oil and a large share of its liquefied natural gas normally passes, toll-free for 60 days. The US naval blockade lifts. Iran gets a $300 billion reconstruction fund and relief from sanctions on its oil exports, and agrees to downgrade its enriched uranium stockpile from weapons-grade to reactor-grade. A further 60 days of ceasefire is built in to negotiate the details.

What the memorandum does not settle is more interesting than what it does. It says nothing specific about dismantling Iran's ballistic missile programme or about Tehran's regional allies such as Hezbollah, and Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu said openly that Israel would keep its "freedom of action" in Lebanon regardless of what Washington and Tehran had agreed. Within days, Israeli strikes on Lebanon were being reported as violations of the deal Trump had just signed.

For India, the practical stakes are the Gulf's oil price and shipping lanes rather than the politics. The Reserve Bank of India cited the West Asia conflict directly when it raised its inflation forecast at its June policy meeting, and a reopened Strait of Hormuz matters to New Delhi almost as much as it does to Washington or Tehran.

topics.title: Supreme Court finds a Fundamental Right to Walk on footpaths
topics.hook: In Maniyar Iliyaz v. P. Ayyappan, the Supreme Court read a fundamental right to walk safely on a demarcated footpath into Article 19(1)(d), the freedom to move freely — a ruling built for a footpath-encroachment fact pattern that any city student recognises.
topics.story:
Article 19(1)(d) of the Constitution guarantees every citizen the right "to move freely throughout the territory of India." For decades courts read this as a right against state restrictions on travel between states or regions — permits, curfews, internal passports. In June 2026, in Maniyar Iliyaz v. P. Ayyappan (2026 SCC OnLine SC 1162), the Supreme Court gave the clause a second, more literal meaning: the primary right of movement, the Court said, is the fundamental right to walk, and it must be exercised on a footpath that is safe and clearly marked off from vehicular traffic.

The case arose out of the kind of dispute Indian cities produce constantly — encroachment on a public footpath that pushed pedestrians into a traffic lane. Rather than treat it as a municipal nuisance matter, the bench framed it as a constitutional question: if Article 19(1)(d) protects movement, and movement for most people in most cities means walking, then the state's failure to maintain walkable, demarcated footpaths is itself a rights violation, not merely bad urban planning.

The judgment sits inside a run of Article 21 and Article 19 cases that have steadily widened positive obligations on the state — the right to clean air, the right to a healthy environment, and now the right to walk safely. It puts municipal corporations and urban development authorities on notice that footpath encroachment and poor pedestrian infrastructure can be challenged in court as a rights matter, not just through a civic complaint.

The ruling landed in the same week the Court swore in five new judges and issued draft regulations on AI use in courtrooms, making the first week of June 2026 an unusually dense one for Indian constitutional law. It is also the kind of judgment CLAT setters like: a familiar constitutional provision, given an unfamiliar and very concrete new reading, decided on facts a 17-year-old in any Indian city has personally experienced.

topics.title: Five new judges take oath at the Supreme Court, including its second woman elevated from the Bar
topics.hook: On 2 June 2026, five new judges — Sheel Nagu, Shree Chandrashekhar, Sanjeev Sachdeva, Arun Palli and V. Mohana — were sworn in to the Supreme Court, with Justice Mohana only the second judge elevated directly from the Bar to the top court.
topics.story:
The President of India appointed five new Supreme Court judges on 1 June 2026, and all five took their oath of office the next day. Four of the five — Sheel Nagu, Shree Chandrashekhar, Sanjeev Sachdeva and Arun Palli — came up through the High Court system, the route almost every Supreme Court judge has followed since 1950. The fifth, V. Mohana, did not.

Justice Mohana was elevated directly from the Bar, meaning she moved from practising as a senior advocate straight to a Supreme Court judgeship without first serving as a High Court judge. This route exists in the Constitution but is rarely used; the first and best-known instance was Justice S.M. Sikri's elevation decades earlier, and appointments made this way are few enough that each one is individually notable. Justice Mohana becomes only the second woman to reach the Supreme Court through direct elevation from the Bar, following in a lineage that has otherwise been almost entirely male.

The appointments follow the collegium system, under which a panel of senior Supreme Court judges recommends names to the government, which then formalises them through presidential appointment. The system has no explicit constitutional basis — it was built up through a series of Supreme Court judgments in the 1990s, collectively called the Judges Cases — and remains one of the more frequently tested features of the Indian judiciary in law-entrance exams, precisely because it is judge-made rather than written into the Constitution's text.

The batch of appointments landed in the same week the Court decided the footpath-movement case and issued its draft AI-in-courts regulations, making early June 2026 a busy stretch for the institution on every front — bench strength, doctrine and technology policy at once.

topics.title: RBI holds rates, cuts growth forecast and moves to shore up the rupee
topics.hook: The RBI's June 2026 Monetary Policy Committee kept the repo rate at 5.25%, cut its FY27 growth forecast to 6.6% and raised its inflation forecast to 5.1%, then rolled out a rupee-support package explicitly citing the West Asia war.
topics.story:
The Monetary Policy Committee, RBI's six-member rate-setting body chaired by the governor, met from 3 to 5 June 2026 and voted unanimously to hold the repo rate at 5.25%, keeping its stance "neutral." The repo rate is the rate at which RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks, and it is the main lever the committee uses to manage inflation and growth; holding it steady signals RBI was neither trying to cool the economy further nor stimulate it. The Standing Deposit Facility rate stayed at 5%, and the Marginal Standing Facility and Bank Rate stayed at 5.5%.

What changed was the outlook. RBI cut its GDP growth forecast for FY 2026-27 to 6.6%, down from the 6.9% it had projected in April, and raised its inflation forecast to 5.1% from 4.6%. It named three reasons directly: the West Asia conflict then still ongoing, higher global energy prices, and uncertainty around the monsoon and El Nino conditions. This was a rare instance of an RBI policy statement naming a specific war as a driver of India's inflation numbers.

Alongside the rate decision, RBI announced measures to defend the rupee. Banks raising fresh three-to-five-year FCNR(B) deposits — foreign-currency deposits held by non-resident Indians — would have their FX hedging costs fully subsidised by RBI. A concessional foreign-exchange swap facility was introduced to encourage public-sector enterprises to raise external commercial borrowings. Both measures aim to pull more foreign currency into the banking system and ease pressure on the rupee.

For context, India's economy grew 7.7% in FY 2025-26, according to the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, meaning the RBI's 6.6% forecast for the following year is a meaningful step down — a rare moment where the RBI is explicitly pricing an ongoing war into its household inflation forecast, not just its language.

topics.title: G7 leaders meet at Evian for the first time in 23 years
topics.hook: France hosted the G7 summit at Evian from 15 to 17 June 2026 — the group's return to the same lakeside town 23 years after it last met there — producing joint statements on growth, critical minerals and child safety online, and providing the backdrop for the Islamabad Memorandum signing.
topics.story:
The Group of Seven — the US, UK, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and Canada, with the EU also represented — held its 2026 summit in Evian-les-Bains, a French town on Lake Geneva that last hosted the group 23 years earlier. France held the rotating G7 presidency for the year and organised the gathering.

The leaders issued several joint statements rather than one single communique: a declaration on balanced and resilient global growth, a call for a safer digital space for minors, a statement on securing supply chains for critical minerals, and separate declarations addressing migrant smuggling and drug trafficking. Critical minerals — lithium, cobalt, rare earths, the raw materials behind batteries, semiconductors and defence technology — have become a recurring G7 theme as members try to reduce dependence on China, which dominates global processing capacity for several of them.

The summit's most consequential moment for global headlines, however, happened on its margins rather than at its formal table. On 17 June, the final day, US president Donald Trump signed the Islamabad Memorandum remotely from the Palace of Versailles, ending the 2026 Iran war, after dining with French president Emmanuel Macron. The G7 summit itself did not negotiate that agreement, but it provided the stage on which it was finalised.

For India, which is not a G7 member but has attended as an invited guest at past summits under the G7's outreach practice, the Evian meeting mattered mainly through its downstream effects: G7 statements on critical minerals and supply chains feed directly into India's own semiconductor and battery-manufacturing push, and the summit's other big story, the Iran deal, shaped RBI's own policy language days later.

topics.title: Delimitation Bill, 2026 fails to pass, government looks to the monsoon session
topics.hook: The Delimitation Bill and its companion constitutional amendment, introduced in April to redraw Lok Sabha seats using the 2011 Census and expand the House to 850 members, failed to secure the numbers in the budget session and is now being pushed to the monsoon session.
topics.story:
Three linked bills were introduced in the Lok Sabha on 16 April 2026: the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, the Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, and the Delimitation Bill itself. Together they would redraw parliamentary constituencies based on the 2011 Census and expand the Lok Sabha from 543 seats to 850 — 815 elected from the states and 35 from union territories. The package also links delimitation to the long-pending 33% reservation for women in the Lok Sabha, since that reservation was designed to be implemented only after the next delimitation exercise.

A constitutional amendment needs a special majority — at least two-thirds of members present and voting in each House, and a majority of the total membership of each House — a much higher bar than an ordinary bill. In the budget session, the government could not muster this, and the bills lapsed for that session without being passed.

By June, the government was reported to be negotiating directly with MPs from the DMK and Trinamool Congress, both of which represent southern and eastern states that stand to gain proportionally fewer new seats than the northern states with faster population growth since 1971 — the reason India froze delimitation at the 1971 Census figures in the first place, precisely to avoid punishing states that had controlled their population growth. The bills are now expected to be reintroduced in the monsoon session.

This is a genuinely difficult political problem, not just a procedural one: any formula based on 2011 or later population figures mechanically shifts seats toward the Hindi-belt states and away from the south, reopening a federalism fight that goes back to the 42nd and 84th Constitutional Amendments, both of which froze delimitation specifically to prevent this outcome.

topics.title: Supreme Court declares rehabilitation a fundamental right for trafficking survivors
topics.hook: In Prajwala v. Union of India, the Supreme Court held that rehabilitation of trafficking survivors is not a discretionary welfare measure but a fundamental right, and ordered a comprehensive, victim-centred protection plan.
topics.story:
Article 23 of the Constitution prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour, one of the few fundamental rights that binds private individuals directly and not just the state. It has rarely been the basis for detailed, structural relief. In Prajwala v. Union of India (2026 SCC OnLine SC 1053), decided in June 2026, the Supreme Court moved beyond simply condemning trafficking as unconstitutional and held that survivors have a fundamental right to rehabilitation, not merely to prosecution of their traffickers.

The petition was brought by Prajwala, an organisation working on anti-trafficking rehabilitation, and the Court's response was to frame trafficking as an assault on human dignity rather than purely a law-and-order or criminal-procedure problem. It adopted what the judgment calls a victim-centric approach, meaning survivors' immediate needs — shelter, medical care, psychological support, economic reintegration — take priority over the pace of criminal trials against traffickers.

The Court issued a comprehensive protection plan rather than leaving implementation to be worked out later by the executive, a pattern that recurs across several of the Court's June 2026 rulings, including its footpath-movement judgment and its order on Chambal sand mining: rather than declaring a right in the abstract, the bench specified the mechanics of enforcement.

This case sits alongside Article 21's right to life with dignity and Article 39(e) and (f), Directive Principles that direct the state to protect children and workers from exploitation. Together they give trafficking litigation multiple constitutional footholds, and this judgment is likely to be cited whenever a state government's rehabilitation scheme for survivors is challenged as inadequate.

topics.title: Lt Gen Dhiraj Seth named the next Chief of the Army Staff
topics.hook: Lieutenant General Dhiraj Seth, then Vice Chief of the Army Staff, was named the next Chief of the Army Staff, effective 30 June 2026 — a straightforward vertical succession that is still worth knowing cold for GK.
topics.story:
The Chief of the Army Staff is the senior-most serving officer of the Indian Army and its professional head, appointed by the President on the recommendation of the government, distinct from the Chief of Defence Staff, who is a newer, tri-services coordinating role created in 2019 and sits above all three service chiefs on inter-service matters without formally commanding troops.

Lieutenant General Dhiraj Seth was serving as Vice Chief of the Army Staff, the second-most senior post in the Army, when he was named to take over as Chief of the Army Staff with effect from 30 June 2026. The Vice Chief traditionally acts as the Army's day-to-day administrative head and is the most common feeder post for the top job, so this was a conventional, expected succession rather than a surprise pick.

Service-chief appointments are a fixture of Indian GK precisely because they change on a predictable annual-to-biennial cycle and because exams test the distinction between the three service chiefs — Army, Navy, Air Force — and the Chief of Defence Staff, a role students frequently conflate with "the senior-most officer overall." The CDS is first among equals on tri-service planning and is the government's principal military adviser, but each service chief still commands their own service independently.

topics.title: Supreme Court prices a homemaker's unpaid work into accident compensation
topics.hook: In Shishu Pal v. Surjeet, the Supreme Court created a new head of compensation, 'Loss of Domestic Care', valuing a homemaker's unpaid household labour at Rs 30,000 a month when calculating motor-accident death claims.
topics.story:
Under the Motor Vehicles Act, compensation for a death in a road accident is generally built around the victim's income — what they earned, and what their dependents lost when that income stopped. This formula has always struggled with homemakers, who are typically unwaged and whose deaths, under a strictly income-based formula, could be valued at close to nothing.

In Shishu Pal v. Surjeet (2026 SCC OnLine SC 1114), decided in June 2026, the Supreme Court addressed this directly. It held that a separate, substantive head of compensation, which it called "Loss of Domestic Care," must be mandatorily factored into the final computation whenever a homemaker dies in a motor accident. The Court set a monthly value of Rs 30,000 for this unpaid domestic labour — cooking, childcare, household management — treating it as economically real rather than symbolic.

The judgment came in the same week as the Court's ruling recognising a fundamental right to walk on footpaths and its order making rehabilitation a fundamental right for trafficking survivors, part of a broader pattern in the Court's early-June 2026 output: taking categories of unpaid, invisible, or under-compensated harm and giving them a concrete legal value or a concrete enforcement mechanism, rather than leaving them as abstract principles.

For law students, the case is a clean example of how compensation law evolves through judicial interpretation of a beneficial statute — the Motor Vehicles Act is explicitly meant to be read generously in favour of claimants, and this ruling is a direct application of that interpretive principle to a gap the legislature had not explicitly filled.

topics.title: India and Pakistan clash again over the Indus Waters Treaty
topics.hook: Pakistan's defence minister said in June 2026 that Pakistan would go to war if it judged its water security genuinely threatened by India's handling of the Indus Waters Treaty — rhetoric that stopped short of action but kept a 1960 treaty back in the headlines.
topics.story:
The Indus Waters Treaty, signed in 1960 between India and Pakistan and brokered by the World Bank, divides the six rivers of the Indus system: India got unrestricted use of the three eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej), and Pakistan got the bulk of the water from the three western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab), with India retaining limited rights for irrigation, hydropower and non-consumptive use on the western rivers. The treaty survived three India-Pakistan wars without either side abrogating it, which is normally cited as one of the more durable pieces of bilateral cooperation between the two countries.

That reputation for durability has been under pressure. On 11 June 2026, Pakistan's Foreign Ministry warned that any Indian move to restrict water flows under the treaty would endanger regional stability, a day after India's water minister C.R. Patil said New Delhi was working to secure its water security. On 19 June, Pakistan's defence minister Khawaja Asif went further, saying Pakistan would go to war if it perceived its water security genuinely threatened by an Indian suspension of the treaty — while also clarifying that current developments did not, in his assessment, warrant military action yet.

The exchange sits against a backdrop that predates June: India suspended elements of its treaty cooperation with Pakistan after the April 2025 Pahalgam terror attack, and has periodically signalled it will use the treaty as leverage in response to cross-border terrorism, a position Pakistan treats as an existential threat given how dependent its agriculture is on the western rivers.

For CLAT purposes, the treaty is a reliable static-GK anchor: 1960, World Bank as broker, the eastern-western river split, and the fact that it has technically survived every war fought since. This June 2026 flare-up is best read as the latest chapter in a long-running story, not a rupture of the treaty itself.

topics.title: The first 48-team FIFA World Cup kicks off across three countries
topics.hook: The 2026 FIFA World Cup opened on 11 June with Mexico's match at Estadio Azteca, the first edition of the tournament expanded to 48 teams and the first jointly hosted by three countries — the United States, Mexico and Canada.
topics.story:
The 2026 FIFA World Cup began on 11 June 2026 with Mexico playing at Estadio Azteca in Mexico City, followed a day later by Canada's opener at BMO Field in Toronto and the United States' opener at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood. It is the first World Cup to be co-hosted by three countries, and the first to use FIFA's new 48-team format, up from the 32 teams that had played every tournament since 1998.

The expanded field is organised into 12 groups of four teams, and the tournament runs to 104 total matches across the group and knockout stages, each team playing three group games. Matches are spread across sixteen host cities: eleven in the United States (including Atlanta, Dallas, Los Angeles, New York/New Jersey and Miami), three in Mexico (Mexico City, Guadalajara, Monterrey), and two in Canada (Toronto, Vancouver). Mexico City's Estadio Azteca becomes the first stadium to host matches at three separate World Cups, having also staged the 1970 and 1986 finals.

The three co-host nations did not fare well on the pitch, despite home advantage: Canada lost to Morocco, Mexico fell to England, and the United States was eliminated by Belgium, all in the Round of 16. Attendance, however, set a new record for the tournament, with nearly 7 million fans across the tournament surpassing the previous high set at USA 1994.

For an Indian student, the exam-relevant hooks are structural rather than result-based: this is the format change (32 to 48 teams), the host-country change (first tri-nation hosting), and the record-attendance fact, all more likely to be tested than any individual match score.

topics.title: Supreme Court issues draft rules for AI use inside courtrooms
topics.hook: The Supreme Court issued draft Regulations for Use of Artificial Intelligence in Courts, 2026, on 3 June, days after separately warning that judges relying on AI-generated fake citations could face misconduct proceedings.
topics.story:
On 3 June 2026, the Supreme Court issued draft Regulations for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Courts, 2026, a proposed framework for how AI tools can be used inside the judicial process — everything from case-management software to AI-assisted legal research — while attempting to protect judicial independence, fairness and constitutional values from being eroded by automation.

The regulations followed closely on a separate but related warning from the Court about a specific failure mode: judges or lawyers relying on non-existent, fake, or AI-hallucinated judgments in judicial decision-making. The Court held that this is not merely a careless error but can amount to professional misconduct, a notably strict line given how often generative AI tools are known to fabricate plausible-looking case citations that do not actually exist.

India is not unique in confronting this problem — courts in several countries have already sanctioned lawyers for filing briefs containing fabricated AI-generated citations — but the Supreme Court's decision to issue standing draft regulations, rather than handling the issue case by case as it arises, is a more structural response. It puts India's apex court among a small group of judiciaries formally regulating AI use in the courtroom rather than reacting to individual incidents.

For CLAT, this connects to two other current threads: India's broader AI governance push (relevant to any question on the IndiaAI Mission or India's position at global AI summits) and the Court's ongoing effort, visible across its June 2026 docket, to modernise procedure without diluting the accountability that judicial reasoning is supposed to carry.

topics.hook: China launched a special maritime enforcement operation east of Taiwan in June 2026, responding to a new Japan-Philippines agreement to negotiate maritime borders and deepen defence cooperation.

topics.title: Draft amendments would cut the poorest households' free foodgrain quota
topics.hook: Draft amendments to the National Food Security Act, floated on 23 June 2026, would change how much subsidised grain the poorest Antyodaya Anna Yojana households get — from 35 kg per household per month to 7 kg per person, a formula that helps large families but can cut allocation for small ones.
topics.story:
The National Food Security Act, 2013, guarantees subsidised foodgrain to roughly two-thirds of India's population through the Public Distribution System, with the poorest households covered under the Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) getting the most generous entitlement. Since the scheme began, AAY entitlement has been fixed per household — 35 kg of grain a month, regardless of how many people live in that household.

Draft amendments proposed on 23 June 2026 would switch this to a per-person formula: 7 kg per person per month. For a household of five or more, this is a straightforward increase — 35 kg becomes 35 kg or more. But for a household of one, two or three people, which is common among elderly or single-member AAY households, 7 kg per person produces a sharp cut from the flat 35 kg they currently receive.

This is the kind of welfare-policy change that sounds technical but has a real distributional bite, and it is the sort of question CLAT likes: not "what is the NFSA" but "who gains and who loses under this specific formula change," which rewards careful reading over memorised definitions.

Thailand's constitutional monarchy has, since a 2014 military coup, cycled through periods of elected civilian government interspersed with military-influenced constitutional arrangements, including a 2017 constitution widely seen as designed to constrain elected majorities relative to appointed institutions such as the Senate. The 2026 general election result was the latest data point in this pattern.

topics.title: RBI bars dark patterns in banking and shifts fraud liability to banks
topics.hook: Through June 2026, RBI issued two consumer-facing rules in quick succession: banning dark patterns and compulsory bundling in banking products on 15 June, then shifting the liability burden for fraudulent transactions onto banks on 24 June.
topics.story:
'Dark patterns' is a term for design tricks — confusing opt-outs, pre-ticked add-ons, hidden fees — that push consumers into choices they would not otherwise make. On 15 June 2026, RBI issued responsible-business-conduct amendments prohibiting dark patterns and restricting compulsory bundling of financial products by banks, meaning a bank can no longer, for instance, tie a loan approval to an unrelated insurance purchase presented as mandatory.

On 24 June, RBI went further on a separate front, amending its framework to shift the liability burden for fraudulent transactions onto banks rather than customers in a wider range of circumstances. Together the two changes move the regulatory weight of digital-banking risk away from individual customers and onto the institutions with more resources and information to prevent it, part of a broader global regulatory trend toward holding platforms and institutions responsible for the harms their design choices or security gaps enable.

passages.title: Ending a war on paper
passages.passage:
The Islamabad Memorandum, signed on 17 June 2026, ended nearly four months of war between Iran, Israel and the United States, but it settled less than its length suggests. The agreement reopens the Strait of Hormuz toll-free for sixty days, lifts the American naval blockade imposed on Iranian ports in April, and offers Iran a $300 billion reconstruction fund along with relief from oil-export sanctions. In exchange, Tehran agreed to downgrade its enriched uranium stockpile from weapons-grade to reactor-grade purity, and both sides accepted a further sixty-day ceasefire window to negotiate remaining details.

What the fourteen-point text does not do is more revealing than what it does. It contains no commitment on Iran's ballistic missile programme and says nothing binding about Tehran's regional allies, chief among them Hezbollah in Lebanon. Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu made clear within hours of the signing that his government considered itself free to continue striking Hezbollah positions regardless of what Washington and Tehran had agreed between themselves, and reports of Israeli strikes on Lebanon soon followed, each one described by observers as a breach of a ceasefire Israel had not, in any binding sense, actually accepted for that front.

This gap between the words of a peace agreement and the conduct of the parties who did not fully sign on to every clause is not new. Ceasefires negotiated between two or three primary belligerents routinely fail to bind the smaller actors whose cooperation was assumed rather than secured, and the Lebanon question in the Islamabad Memorandum sits squarely in that pattern. Pakistan and Qatar, the memorandum's chief mediators, have no direct leverage over Hezbollah or Israeli decision-making, and the document's silence on both suggests its authors knew that. The reopening of Hormuz and the economic terms address the interests of Iran, the US and the oil-consuming world directly. The Lebanon front, and the militia fighting on it, remain outside the paper's actual reach — a fact the ink on the page cannot change, whatever the headlines announcing peace choose to say.

questions.q: Which of the following best captures the main argument of the passage?
options: The Islamabad Memorandum was a total failure that changed nothing
The memorandum ended fighting on fronts its main signatories controlled, but could not bind actors like Hezbollah who were not full parties to it
Israel refused to sign the memorandum at all
Pakistan and Qatar deliberately sabotaged the Lebanon provisions
questions.explain: The passage's central point is the gap between the memorandum's formal scope and its actual binding power over parties like Hezbollah and Israel's Lebanon operations. Option A overstates failure — the passage credits the deal with reopening Hormuz and lifting the blockade. Options C and D are not supported by the text.

questions.q: According to the passage, why does the memorandum's silence on Hezbollah make sense as a negotiating outcome?
options: Because Hezbollah was invited to sign but refused
Because Pakistan and Qatar, the chief mediators, had no direct leverage over Hezbollah or Israel's decisions
Because the memorandum was only ever meant to cover Iran's nuclear programme
Because Israel is not a party to the Strait of Hormuz provisions
questions.explain: The passage explicitly states that the mediators lacked direct leverage over Hezbollah or Israeli decision-making, which explains the gap. There is no mention of Hezbollah being invited to sign (A), and the memorandum covers more than the nuclear programme (C).

questions.q: Which of the following is stated in the passage as true?
options: The memorandum includes binding commitments on Iran's ballistic missile programme
The Strait of Hormuz reopening is permanent and unconditional
Iran agreed to downgrade its uranium stockpile from weapons-grade to reactor-grade
The ceasefire window built into the memorandum lasts one year
questions.explain: The passage states Iran agreed to the uranium downgrade. It explicitly says the missile programme is not addressed (contradicting A), the Hormuz reopening is for sixty days, not permanent (contradicting B), and the additional ceasefire window is sixty days, not a year (contradicting D).

questions.q: The passage implies that ceasefires between primary belligerents often struggle to bind smaller actors because:
options: Smaller actors are always excluded from negotiations deliberately
Their cooperation is often assumed by negotiators rather than actually secured through direct engagement
International law does not recognise non-state actors
Smaller actors typically have stronger military capability than the main signatories
questions.explain: The passage says this pattern occurs because such actors' cooperation 'was assumed rather than secured' — a specific claim about negotiating failure, not deliberate exclusion (A) or a legal technicality (C), and it says nothing about relative military strength (D).

The 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), which the US withdrew from in 2018
The 1968 Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty's original signing

questions.explain: The JCPOA of 2015 was the major prior international agreement specifically negotiating limits on Iran's nuclear programme, and the US withdrawal from it in 2018 is the direct historical precedent for this kind of deal-making and its fragility. passages.title: A right rediscovered on the pavement
passages.passage:
Article 19(1)(d) of the Constitution has sat in the text since 1950, guaranteeing every citizen the right to move freely throughout Indian territory. For most of its life, courts read this as a shield against state-imposed barriers to travel — checkpoints, internal permits, movement restrictions between regions. In June 2026, the Supreme Court gave the clause a use nobody had quite framed this way before: in Maniyar Iliyaz v. P. Ayyappan, the Court held that the primary right of movement is the fundamental right to walk, and that this right must be exercisable on a footpath safe and clearly demarcated from vehicular traffic.

The case began as an ordinary municipal dispute — encroachment on a public footpath that forced pedestrians into a traffic lane. The bench declined to treat it as a matter for a civic complaint alone. If Article 19(1)(d) protects movement, the Court reasoned, and if walking is how most people in most Indian cities actually move, then a city's failure to maintain safe, walkable footpaths becomes a constitutional failure and not merely poor urban planning.

This is not the first time the Supreme Court has read a positive obligation into a right that originally looked like a negative restraint on government power. The right to clean air and the right to a healthy environment were built the same way, out of Article 21's guarantee of life and personal liberty, over a series of judgments stretching back decades. What makes the footpath case notable is which article did the work: not Article 21, the usual vehicle for this kind of expansion, but Article 19(1)(d), a clause more often associated with interstate travel restrictions than with municipal infrastructure. Municipal corporations across India, the ruling implies, can now face rights-based litigation over pedestrian infrastructure, not just administrative complaints that move at the pace of local bureaucracy.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Article 21 has always covered footpath safety
The Supreme Court used Article 19(1)(d), traditionally read as protecting interstate travel, to establish a constitutional right to safe footpaths
Municipal corporations are immune from litigation over footpaths
The case concerned a dispute between two private citizens with no constitutional dimension
questions.explain: The passage's core point is the reinterpretation of Article 19(1)(d) — usually about interstate movement — to cover footpath safety, marking an unusual doctrinal move. Option A is wrong since the passage says Article 21 was NOT the vehicle used here; the passage explicitly frames this as a departure from that expected pattern.

questions.q: The passage suggests that the Court's approach to Article 19(1)(d) is unusual because:
options: It is the first time any fundamental right has been expanded through interpretation
This kind of positive-obligation reading is usually built through Article 21, not Article 19(1)(d)
The clause had never been interpreted by any court before
Article 19(1)(d) applies only to non-citizens
questions.explain: The passage states this pattern of expansion is 'usually' done through Article 21, making the choice of Article 19(1)(d) notable. It does not claim this is the first-ever rights expansion (A), nor that the clause was never interpreted before (C); D is factually wrong since Article 19 rights apply to citizens.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is true according to the passage?
options: The footpath case began as a constitutional petition filed directly in the Supreme Court on Article 19 grounds
The case originated from an encroachment dispute that the Court chose to treat as a constitutional matter
The Supreme Court refused to hear the footpath case
Article 19(1)(d) was added to the Constitution after 1950
questions.explain: The passage says the case 'began as an ordinary municipal dispute' over encroachment, which the bench then treated as constitutional rather than merely civic. Article 19(1)(d) has been in the Constitution since it came into force in 1950, contradicting D.

questions.q: Which inference about municipal corporations is best supported by the passage?
options: They are now fully exempt from footpath-related lawsuits
They may now face constitutional, rights-based challenges over footpath maintenance, in addition to ordinary civic complaints
They no longer have any legal obligation regarding footpaths
They must seek Supreme Court approval before building any footpath
questions.explain: The passage states municipal corporations 'can now face rights-based litigation over pedestrian infrastructure, not just administrative complaints' — implying an additional, higher-stakes avenue of challenge, not exemption or a pre-approval requirement.

questions.q: A separate June 2026 development saw five new judges take their oath at the Supreme Court. Which appointment mechanism governs how such judges are typically selected?
options: Direct election by sitting High Court judges
The collegium system, a judge-made process without explicit textual basis in the Constitution
Appointment solely by the Chief Justice without government involvement
A public examination administered by the Union Public Service Commission
questions.explain: India's collegium system, developed through Supreme Court rulings in the 1990s (the Judges Cases), governs judicial appointments and has no explicit basis in the Constitution's text — a fact tested alongside the five-judges appointment story. The other options describe mechanisms not used for Supreme Court appointments in India.

passages.title: Holding steady while the outlook shifts
passages.passage:
When the Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee met from 3 to 5 June 2026, it made a decision that on its face looked like no decision at all: the repo rate stayed exactly where it had been, at 5.25%, and the policy stance remained 'neutral.' Beneath that stillness, however, the committee's outlook moved considerably. It cut its growth forecast for the coming financial year to 6.6%, down from the 6.9% it had projected only two months earlier, and it raised its inflation forecast to 5.1% from 4.6%.

The committee named its reasons plainly: the West Asia conflict then still unresolved, elevated global energy prices, and uncertainty surrounding the monsoon. This is an unusual level of specificity for a central bank statement, which more often gestures at 'global headwinds' without naming a particular war. The explicitness reflected how directly the conflict was feeding into India's energy import bill and, through it, into domestic prices.

Alongside the rate decision, the RBI moved on a second front entirely: defending the rupee. It announced it would fully subsidise the foreign-exchange hedging costs of banks raising fresh three-to-five-year FCNR(B) deposits, a category of foreign-currency accounts held by non-resident Indians, and introduced a concessional currency-swap facility to encourage public-sector enterprises to raise money abroad. Both measures share a single goal: pulling more foreign currency into India's banking system at a moment when the war-driven cost of energy imports was placing pressure on the currency from the other direction. None of this changed the headline number the news carried the same week: India's GDP had grown 7.7% in the financial year that had just ended, a figure the RBI's own more cautious forecast for the year ahead was measured directly against.

questions.q: What is the main point the passage makes about the RBI's June 2026 policy meeting?
options: The RBI cut interest rates sharply to boost growth
The RBI held the repo rate steady while significantly revising its growth and inflation outlook, and separately acted to support the rupee
The RBI raised the repo rate to control inflation
The RBI's meeting produced no changes of any kind
questions.explain: The passage's structure makes clear the repo rate itself was unchanged, but the outlook (growth down, inflation up) shifted, and separate rupee-support measures were announced — a combination captured only by option B.

questions.q: Why does the passage describe the RBI's naming of the West Asia conflict as 'an unusual level of specificity'?
options: Because central banks never discuss geopolitical events
Because central banks more often refer vaguely to 'global headwinds' rather than naming a specific conflict
Because the RBI is legally barred from mentioning foreign wars
Because the conflict had already ended by the time of the statement
questions.explain: The passage directly contrasts this specificity with the more typical vague reference to 'global headwinds.' The conflict had not ended by June 5 (the ceasefire came on June 17), so D is factually wrong per the passage's own timeline elsewhere in this file.

questions.q: Which of the following is true according to the passage?
options: FCNR(B) deposits are foreign-currency accounts held by non-resident Indians
The RBI raised the repo rate to 5.25% from a lower level
India's GDP grew at a rate lower than the RBI's forecast for the following year
The monsoon played no role in the RBI's inflation forecast
questions.explain: The passage explicitly defines FCNR(B) deposits this way. The repo rate was held, not raised (contradicting B); GDP growth (7.7%) was actually higher than the following year's forecast (6.6%), not lower (contradicting C); and monsoon uncertainty was one of the three named reasons (contradicting D).

questions.q: What can be inferred about the relationship between the Iran war and India's currency management in June 2026?
options: The war had no effect on India's foreign exchange policy
The war's effect on energy prices created pressure on the rupee, prompting RBI's currency-support measures
The RBI stopped managing the rupee entirely during the conflict
India banned all foreign currency transactions during the war
questions.explain: The passage links the war-driven energy import costs directly to rupee pressure, which the RBI's FCNR(B) and swap measures were designed to offset — an inference drawn from connecting two paragraphs of the passage, not stated in one single sentence.

questions.q: India's central bank sets its key policy rate through a specific institutional body. Which body is this, and how many members does it typically have?
options: The Finance Ministry's Budget Division, with no fixed membership
The Monetary Policy Committee, a six-member body chaired by the RBI governor
The Reserve Bank's Board of Directors, with fifteen members
The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs, chaired by the Prime Minister
questions.explain: The Monetary Policy Committee is the specific six-member, governor-chaired body responsible for setting the repo rate in India — background static knowledge the passage assumes but does not spell out in full.

passages.title: Counting heads, redrawing lines
passages.passage:
Three bills, introduced together in the Lok Sabha on 16 April 2026, set out to do something India has avoided doing for more than half a century: redraw its parliamentary constituencies using current population data. The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, the Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, and the Delimitation Bill together propose expanding the Lok Sabha from 543 seats to 850, using the 2011 Census as the population base, with 815 seats allocated to the states and 35 to union territories. Tied to this expansion is the long-delayed 33% reservation for women in the Lok Sabha, a reform designed from the outset to take effect only once a fresh delimitation exercise was complete.

The reason India froze delimitation in the first place is itself a piece of constitutional history worth knowing. The 42nd and later the 84th Constitutional Amendments locked seat allocation to 1971 Census figures, specifically to prevent states that had successfully slowed population growth — largely in the south — from being penalised with fewer seats relative to states that had not. Any formula using 2011 or more recent figures mechanically shifts parliamentary weight toward the faster-growing, largely northern states, which is exactly the outcome the 1971 freeze was designed to avoid.

Because these are constitutional amendment bills, they require a special majority to pass — at least two-thirds of members present and voting in each House, along with a majority of each House's total membership, a considerably higher bar than an ordinary law needs. In the 2026 budget session, the government could not clear this threshold, and the bills lapsed for that session. By June, reports suggested the government was negotiating directly with MPs from the DMK and Trinamool Congress, two parties representing states with the most to lose under a 2011-based formula, in an effort to build the numbers needed before the bills are reintroduced in the monsoon session.

questions.q: What is the central problem the passage describes?
options: India has never attempted to reform its parliamentary seat allocation
A population-based redrawing of Lok Sabha seats is politically difficult because it would shift seats away from states that controlled population growth
The Delimitation Bill has already been passed and implemented
The bill only affects union territories, not states
questions.explain: The passage's central tension is the political difficulty of a population-based reform given its effect on southern states — captured only by option B. The bills have not passed (contradicting C), and they explicitly cover states as well as UTs (contradicting D).

questions.q: Why, according to the passage, was delimitation frozen at 1971 Census figures in the first place?
options: To punish states with declining populations
To prevent states that had successfully slowed population growth from losing relative seat share
Because the 1971 Census was more accurate than later censuses
Because the Constitution originally prohibited any delimitation after 1971
questions.explain: The passage states this directly: the freeze aimed to avoid penalising population-control success, mostly benefiting southern states. There is no claim in the passage about accuracy (C) or an original constitutional prohibition (D).

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the bills' passage requirements is correct?
options: They need only a simple majority in the Lok Sabha
They need a special majority: two-thirds present and voting, plus a majority of total membership, in each House
They can be passed by an executive order without Parliament
They require ratification by all state legislatures before introduction
questions.explain: The passage explicitly defines this special-majority requirement, which is why the government could not pass the bills in the budget session. Constitutional amendments affecting federal structure sometimes need state ratification, but the passage does not state this is required before introduction, and simple majority (A) is insufficient for a constitutional amendment.

questions.q: What can be inferred about why the government was negotiating with the DMK and Trinamool Congress specifically?
options: These parties control the largest number of union territory seats
These parties represent southern and eastern states that would lose relative seat share under a 2011-based formula, making their support politically necessary
These parties support the bill unconditionally and needed no persuasion
These parties are part of the ruling coalition and their support was already guaranteed
questions.explain: The passage identifies DMK and TMC as representing states 'with the most to lose' under the new formula, implying their resistance is precisely why the government needed to negotiate with them rather than assume support.

questions.q: The bills propose tying the implementation of a major social reform to the completion of delimitation. Which reform is this, and what fraction of seats does it involve?
options: Reservation for Scheduled Castes, at 15% of seats
Reservation for women in the Lok Sabha, at 33% of seats
Reservation for Other Backward Classes, at 27% of seats
Reservation for persons with disabilities, at 3% of seats
questions.explain: The passage names the 33% women's reservation in the Lok Sabha as the reform tied to delimitation's completion — a specific figure worth remembering distinctly from the SC/ST/OBC reservation percentages tested elsewhere in static polity questions.

passages.title: A 1960 treaty, back in the headlines
passages.passage:
For sixty-six years, the Indus Waters Treaty has done something unusual in India-Pakistan relations: survived. Signed in 1960 and brokered by the World Bank, the treaty divides the six rivers of the Indus system between the two countries. India received unrestricted use of the three eastern rivers, the Ravi, Beas and Sutlej. Pakistan received the bulk of the water from the three western rivers, the Indus, Jhelum and Chenab, though India retained limited rights on these for irrigation, hydropower and other non-consumptive purposes. The treaty remained formally in force through the wars of 1965, 1971 and 1999, a fact regularly cited as evidence that some forms of bilateral cooperation can outlast even armed conflict between the same two states.

That reputation came under renewed strain in June 2026. On 11 June, Pakistan's Foreign Ministry warned that any Indian move to restrict water flows under the treaty would endanger regional stability, a statement issued a day after India's water minister, C.R. Patil, said New Delhi was working to secure its own water security. The exchange escalated further on 19 June, when Pakistan's defence minister, Khawaja Asif, said Pakistan would go to war if it judged its water security genuinely threatened by an Indian suspension of the treaty — while adding, in the same breath, that current developments did not yet warrant military action.

That caveat matters. Asif's statement was conditional and hypothetical rather than a declaration of intent, and it followed a pattern that predates June 2026: India has periodically signalled it will treat the treaty as leverage in response to cross-border terrorism, most notably suspending elements of cooperation after the April 2025 Pahalgam attack, without formally abrogating the agreement itself. The June exchange reads less as a rupture than as the latest round of a long-running contest over how much pressure the treaty can absorb before one side actually acts on its rhetoric.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: The Indus Waters Treaty collapsed entirely in June 2026
Despite renewed and sharp rhetoric in June 2026, the Indus Waters Treaty had not actually been suspended or abrogated by either side
Pakistan declared war on India over water rights in June 2026
India and Pakistan have never had any dispute over the Indus Waters Treaty before 2026
questions.explain: The passage's closing paragraph makes clear the June 2026 exchange was escalatory rhetoric, not an actual rupture — matching option B. No war was declared (contradicting C), and the passage explicitly notes a history of prior tension (contradicting D).

questions.q: According to the passage, which rivers did India receive unrestricted use of under the 1960 treaty?
options: The Indus, Jhelum and Chenab
The Ravi, Beas and Sutlej
All six rivers of the Indus system
The Ganges and its tributaries
questions.explain: The passage states these are the three eastern rivers allocated to India's unrestricted use; the Indus, Jhelum and Chenab went mostly to Pakistan, and the Ganges is unrelated to this treaty.

questions.q: Why does the passage highlight Khawaja Asif's caveat that 'current developments did not yet warrant military action'?
options: To show that Pakistan had already begun military mobilisation
To indicate that his statement was conditional rather than an announcement of imminent conflict
Because the caveat was a mistranslation with no real significance
To prove that India had formally abrogated the treaty
questions.explain: The passage explicitly says 'that caveat matters' and explains it makes the statement conditional and hypothetical, directly supporting option B. Nothing in the passage suggests mobilisation (A) or mistranslation (C), and India had not abrogated the treaty (D).

questions.q: Which inference about the treaty's history is best supported by the passage?
options: The treaty has never faced any strain since 1960
The treaty's survival through three wars is notable precisely because bilateral cooperation of any kind is otherwise rare between India and Pakistan during conflict
The treaty was renegotiated after each war
The World Bank withdrew as broker after the 1971 war
questions.explain: The passage frames the treaty's wartime survival as 'unusual' and 'regularly cited as evidence' of exceptional durability, implying such cooperation is otherwise rare — supporting option B. No renegotiation or World Bank withdrawal is mentioned.

questions.q: The passage refers to the April 2025 Pahalgam attack as background to India's position. What kind of document usually formalises a country's decision to fully exit a bilateral treaty like this one, as opposed to merely suspending elements of cooperation?
options: A unilateral notice of treaty abrogation or withdrawal, communicated formally to the other party and/or the treaty's broker
An internal parliamentary resolution with no external communication required
A private diplomatic cable with no legal effect
A judicial ruling by the International Court of Justice
questions.explain: Formal treaty exit generally requires an explicit notice of withdrawal or abrogation communicated to the other party and any broker, distinct from merely pausing cooperation informally — the distinction the passage relies on to argue India has not gone that far. This is outside-knowledge the passage only gestures at through its own careful wording.

passages.title: A formula change that helps some and hurts others
passages.passage:
Since the National Food Security Act came into force in 2013, India's poorest identified households, those covered under the Antyodaya Anna Yojana, have received a fixed monthly entitlement of 35 kilograms of subsidised grain — a flat amount, regardless of how many people live under that roof. Draft amendments floated in June 2026 propose replacing this household-based formula with a per-person one: 7 kilograms per person, per month.

On its face, this looks like a technical adjustment, the kind of bureaucratic change that rarely makes headlines. Its actual effect depends entirely on household size, which the flat formula never accounted for and the new one directly addresses. A household of five or more people would see its entitlement rise: 7 kilograms multiplied by five is 35, and any additional member pushes the total higher than the old flat rate ever allowed. But a household of one, two or three people — common among elderly beneficiaries living alone, or small families identified as among the poorest — would see a sharp reduction. A single-person AAY household, for instance, would drop from 35 kilograms a month to just 7.

This is precisely the kind of policy change that a purely definitional understanding of the National Food Security Act will not help a student answer. Knowing that the Act covers roughly two-thirds of India's population through the Public Distribution System, or that AAY is its most generous category, tells a reader nothing about who specifically gains and who specifically loses under this particular formula change. The answer lies entirely in arithmetic: multiply the per-person rate by household size, and compare the result to the flat rate it would replace.

questions.q: What is the main point of the passage?
options: The National Food Security Act was repealed in June 2026
A proposed shift from a household-based to a per-person entitlement formula would raise benefits for large AAY households and cut them for small ones
All AAY households would receive more grain under the new formula
The passage argues the amendment should not be implemented
questions.explain: The passage's core argument is the differential effect based on household size, explicitly illustrated with the five-person and one-person examples — matching option B precisely. Option C is contradicted by the passage's own single-person example.

questions.q: According to the passage, how much would a single-person AAY household receive under the proposed formula?
options: 35 kilograms per month, unchanged
7 kilograms per month
14 kilograms per month
No grain at all
questions.explain: The passage states this explicitly: 'A single-person AAY household...would drop from 35 kilograms a month to just 7.'

questions.q: The passage argues that a household of five or more would benefit from the new formula because:
options: Large households are exempt from the formula entirely
7 kilograms multiplied by five equals 35, and additional members push the total above the old flat rate
The government offers a special bonus to large families
Large households were previously excluded from AAY coverage
questions.explain: The passage does this exact multiplication to show why five-plus-member households gain under the new formula, directly supporting option B.

questions.q: What does the passage suggest about how a student should approach this kind of policy question?
options: Memorise the definition of the National Food Security Act and nothing else
Understand the specific numerical formula and calculate its effect on different household sizes, since general definitional knowledge alone is insufficient
Assume all welfare policy changes reduce benefits
Ignore household size as an irrelevant detail
questions.explain: The passage's final paragraph explicitly states that 'a purely definitional understanding...will not help' and that 'the answer lies entirely in arithmetic' involving household size — directly supporting option B.

questions.q: The National Food Security Act is implemented through a nationwide distribution network. What is this network commonly called?
options: The Direct Benefit Transfer system
The Public Distribution System (PDS)
The National Rural Employment Guarantee network
The Integrated Child Development Services network
questions.explain: The Public Distribution System, mentioned in the passage as the delivery mechanism covering roughly two-thirds of India's population, is the correct answer; the other schemes named serve entirely different purposes (employment guarantee, child development) unrelated to foodgrain distribution.

passages.title: A summit remembered for what happened on its margins
passages.passage:
France hosted the Group of Seven's 2026 summit in Evian-les-Bains, a lakeside town on the French side of Lake Geneva, from 15 to 17 June — the group's return to the same venue twenty-three years after it had last met there. The G7 comprises the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and Canada, with the European Union also represented at its meetings, and India, while not a member, has in past years attended select sessions as an invited guest under the group's outreach practice.

The Evian gathering produced a cluster of joint statements rather than a single unified communique: declarations on balanced and resilient global growth, on securing supply chains for critical minerals such as lithium, cobalt and rare earths, on creating a safer digital environment for minors online, and on tackling migrant smuggling and drug trafficking. The critical-minerals statement, in particular, reflected a now-familiar G7 anxiety: heavy dependence on Chinese processing capacity for the raw materials that go into batteries, semiconductors and defence technology.

Yet the summit's most consequential news did not come from any of its formal sessions. On its final day, 17 June, the fighting between the United States, Iran and Israel that had defined the first half of 2026 came to a formal, if incomplete, end. US President Donald Trump signed the Islamabad Memorandum remotely from the Palace of Versailles, having spent the evening at dinner with French President Emmanuel Macron. The G7 itself had not negotiated the deal — Pakistan and Qatar had done that work over the preceding months — but the summit happened to provide the room, the cameras and the moment in which it was finally made official.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: The G7 summit at Evian formally negotiated and mediated the Islamabad Memorandum
While the G7 summit at Evian addressed its own agenda, its most notable outcome was the coincidental signing of the Islamabad Memorandum on its sidelines
India hosted the G7 summit in 2026
The G7 summit failed to produce any joint statements
questions.explain: The passage draws a clear distinction between the summit's own formal agenda and the memorandum signing, explicitly noting the G7 'had not negotiated the deal' but merely provided the setting — matching option B precisely.

questions.q: According to the passage, which countries actually negotiated the Islamabad Memorandum?
options: The G7 member states collectively
Pakistan and Qatar
India and China
The United Nations Security Council
questions.explain: The passage states plainly that 'Pakistan and Qatar had done that work over the preceding months,' distinguishing the mediators from the G7 summit where the signing occurred.

questions.q: Which of the following is stated as true in the passage?
options: India is a full member of the G7
The G7 includes the United States, United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and Canada, with the EU also represented
The 2026 summit was Evian's first time hosting a G7 meeting
The summit produced a single unified communique rather than multiple statements
questions.explain: This membership list is stated directly in the passage. India is explicitly described as a non-member guest (contradicting A); Evian had hosted a G7 summit 23 years earlier (contradicting C); and the passage says the summit produced 'a cluster of joint statements rather than a single unified communique' (contradicting D).

questions.q: What does the passage imply is the underlying concern behind the G7's critical-minerals statement?
options: A shortage of gold reserves among G7 members
Heavy dependence on Chinese processing capacity for materials used in batteries, semiconductors and defence technology
A dispute over Antarctic mineral rights
Declining global demand for lithium
questions.explain: The passage explicitly names this dependence on Chinese processing capacity as the 'familiar G7 anxiety' behind the statement — the only option grounded directly in the text.

questions.q: The passage notes India has attended past G7 summits as an invited guest. Which broader diplomatic practice does this reflect?
options: G7 outreach or 'plus' sessions inviting major non-member economies to selected discussions
A formal expansion of G7 membership to include India permanently
A rotating G7 chairmanship shared with non-member states
A requirement that all G20 members automatically attend G7 summits
questions.explain: The G7's practice of inviting non-member economies like India to specific outreach sessions, without granting full membership, is the correct background fact — distinct from a permanent membership expansion (B) or any G20-G7 automatic linkage (D), which do not exist.

passages.title: Putting a number on unpaid work
passages.passage:
Compensation for a death in a road accident, under India's Motor Vehicles Act, has traditionally been built around a simple idea: measure what the deceased earned, and calculate what their dependents lost when that income disappeared. The formula has always struggled with one category of victim in particular — homemakers, whose labour, though economically real, has rarely been waged, and who, under a strictly income-based calculation, risked being valued at close to nothing.

In June 2026, the Supreme Court addressed this gap directly. In Shishu Pal v. Surjeet, the Court created a new, mandatory head of compensation it called 'Loss of Domestic Care,' setting its value at 30,000 rupees a month, to be factored into every compensation calculation involving the death of a homemaker. The ruling did not treat this as a symbolic or discretionary gesture; the Court held the head must be included, not merely considered.

The judgment did not arrive in isolation. The same week, in a separate case, the Court held that rehabilitation is a fundamental right for survivors of human trafficking, not a matter of state discretion, and ordered a detailed, victim-centred protection plan rather than leaving implementation to be worked out later. Read together, the two rulings share a method as much as a spirit: rather than declaring a right or a harm in the abstract and trusting the executive or lower courts to fill in the details, the Court specified the mechanics itself — a rupee figure in one case, a structured plan in the other. Both rulings interpret existing, often decades-old legal frameworks — the Motor Vehicles Act's compensation provisions and Article 23's prohibition of trafficking — generously, treating them as living instruments capable of recognising forms of harm the original drafters may not have specifically anticipated.

questions.q: What is the main idea connecting the two rulings described in the passage?
options: Both rulings reduced compensation available to victims
Both rulings specified concrete enforcement mechanics rather than declaring rights in the abstract, applying existing legal frameworks generously to previously under-recognised harms
Both rulings concerned disputes over property inheritance
Both rulings were overturned on appeal within the same month
questions.explain: The passage's final paragraph explicitly draws this connection — a shared method of specifying mechanics rather than abstract declarations, and generous interpretation of existing statutes. No mention is made of reduced compensation, property disputes, or an appeal overturning either ruling.

questions.q: According to the passage, what monthly value did the Supreme Court assign to 'Loss of Domestic Care'?
questions.explain: The passage states this figure directly: 'setting its value at 30,000 rupees a month.'

questions.q: The passage states the 'Loss of Domestic Care' head must be:
options: Considered only if the claimant specifically requests it
Included as a discretionary bonus at the court's option
Mandatorily factored into every relevant compensation calculation
Excluded in cases where the homemaker had any other source of income
questions.explain: The passage is explicit: 'the Court held the head must be included, not merely considered' — ruling out discretion (B) and any request-based trigger (A). No income-based exclusion (D) is mentioned.

questions.q: Which inference about the trafficking-rehabilitation ruling is best supported by the passage?
options: The Court left rehabilitation entirely to the discretion of state governments
The Court treated rehabilitation as a right requiring a specific, structured implementation plan rather than a vague entitlement
The ruling concerned only the prosecution of traffickers, not survivor welfare
The ruling was decided in a different month from the Loss of Domestic Care case
questions.explain: The passage states the Court 'ordered a detailed, victim-centred protection plan rather than leaving implementation to be worked out later,' directly supporting option B, and both cases are described as decided 'the same week.'

questions.q: The passage notes both rulings interpret 'existing, often decades-old legal frameworks' generously. Which interpretive principle in Indian law describes reading a welfare-oriented statute broadly in favour of the persons it is meant to protect?
options: The doctrine of pith and substance
The beneficial-legislation interpretive principle
The doctrine of colourable legislation
The rule of harmonious construction between two unrelated statutes
questions.explain: The beneficial-legislation principle specifically directs courts to interpret welfare statutes, like the Motor Vehicles Act's compensation provisions, generously in favour of claimants — the concept the passage gestures at without naming outright. The other doctrines listed concern legislative competence and statutory conflict, not beneficial interpretation.
